chapter_theme: The Kailasa verses are a series of 'when?' questions that draw the renouncer's life the poet wants: having left home, begging when hunger comes, toothless and white-mouthed, with no attachment and no word or meaning left, sleeping in bliss; free of thought, liking, act, remembering and not-remembering; standing in the Lord's presence with hair bristling and tears running down the chest; not flattering the rich; carried like a kitten by its mother; drinking the honey of the five letters in the company of the good. The closing Madurai verse asks whether any of this is possible without grace.
structure_note: 320 opens with a plea to end birth; 321 to 325 each end என்றோ or என்றிருப்பேன் (when will it be?), to the Lord of Kailasa; 326 and 327 shift from asking to stating what the poet is and will not do; 328, addressed to Sokkanatha of Madurai, is a string of விடப்படுமோ questions on the same pattern as 313.

320.reading: King of the silver mountain where the forests lean, I have trusted your anklet-feet; end the birth in which flesh wastes away. Siva-sprout who, for the man of Kavur, leaned your good holy body, so that the deer leaned, the axe in your red hand leaned and the honey of the konrai you wear ran down.
320.nuance: The verse is built on சாய (to lean, to bend) in every line. காவூரனுக்காய் ... திருமேனி சாய்த்த refers to some occasion on which Siva bent his body for a devotee of Kavur, a story I cannot place; the plain sense is that the Lord who once stooped for one devotee is asked to end this one's birth.

321.reading: Having left the house, standing and begging there when hunger comes, my teeth gone and my mouth white, with no hold on anything, having lost both word and meaning, in the sleep of blissful ease: when will I be so, night and day, Lord of Kailasa?
321.nuance: The renunciation wished for is not dignified: toothless, white-mouthed, begging. சொல்லும் பொருளும் இழந்து, losing word and meaning, is both the wreck of speech in old age and the yogic end of language; சுகானந்தத் தூக்கம், the sleep of bliss, is named again at 322 as ஆனந்த நித்திரை.

322.reading: Free of thought, free of liking, free of action, free of what was thought and free of not-thinking, without thought, alone with myself, in the drowse in which the sleep of bliss settles: when will I stay so, Father, Lord of Kailasa?
322.nuance: The verse removes thought and then removes its absence too (நினைந்ததும் அற்று நினையாமையும் அற்று), so the state is not blankness but something past the pair. அனந்தல், drowsiness, is a plain word for a state the Tirumanthiram calls samadhi; the poet keeps the homely image of sleep.

323.reading: Having received with full hands and eaten standing there, wearing an unstitched black cloth, coming always to your presence, bowing with my whole body, the hair bristling within me, crying out 'Aiya': when will that be, Lord of Kailasa?
323.nuance: கரித்துணியைத் தையாது உடுத்து, wearing a dark cloth without stitching it, is the one outward mark the poet allows himself, set beside the bodily signs of devotion, bristling hair and the cry. The body that bows (மெய்யார நிற்பணிந்து) is the same body 319 reviled.

324.reading: The ash-smeared body's hair bristling, the heart breaking and breaking and softening to mud, melting and melting, in unchanging meditation on your glorious feet, taking on bliss, tears swelling into a river down the chest: when will I get this, Lord of Kailasa?
324.nuance: The sequence is the standard Saiva physiology of devotion, ash, bristling, melting, tears, but the poet asks for it as a gift (கிடைப்பது என்றோ), not as something he can produce. நெக்குநெக்கு and கசிந்து கசிந்து double the verbs of melting that the Tirumanthiram makes the one condition of reaching the Lord.

325.reading: Not going after the rich to speak of my hardship and show my teeth day after day in anxiety, but entering the bound of supreme bliss in a solitude that is a place for me, free of trouble: when will I stay so, Father, Lord of Kailasa?
325.nuance: பல்லினைக் காட்டி, showing the teeth, is the forced grin of the suppliant. The verse distinguishes the begging of 321 and 323, which is from anyone when hungry, from courting the rich, which it refuses; the alternative is ஏகாந்தம், solitude, as the place of bliss.

326.reading: I am not the monkey's young, which holds on by itself; a dog, though I know the custom, what can I do with a mind that keeps on thinking? Drive the evil from me and, like the cat that carries its kitten when they part, you are the one who belongs to my father, Lord of Kailasa.
326.nuance: The pair of images is the later Vaishnava and Saiva figure for two kinds of grace: the monkey's cub clings to its mother by its own effort, the kitten is carried by the cat. The poet says he is not the clinging cub, so must be carried. மந்திக் குருளை அத்தேன் இல்லை is read as 'I am not that (cub)'; the text is loose, and எந்தைக்கு உரியவன் (the one who belongs to my father) is obscure, perhaps 'you who are mine as a father'.

327.reading: I will not be born and die again and go the way of the deluding senses to grieve; I will not enter hell; I have stayed where those who praise you are, and I will not leave the company of the good; by your grace I will drink the rare honey that is the five letters, Lord of Kailasa.
327.nuance: After six verses of 'when?', the poet speaks in the future indicative: not born, not in hell, not leaving the company. The ground given is twofold, the company of the good already joined and the grace still to come, and the five letters are drunk as honey rather than recited.

328.reading: Can this worldly life be given up? Having given it up, can the mind grow firm? Without your grace, can the daily wandering be crossed? Must I go to the gates of the petty and suffer with tears welling? Sokkanatha, Sundara Pandya.
328.nuance: The questions of the first three lines are answered by the third's condition: none of it is possible without grace. The fourth line, standing at the door of the petty, is the fate the poet fears for one who leaves the world without grace, the same begging from the rich that 325 refuses. Sundara Pandya is Siva as the Pandya king of Madurai.

links.note: Both describe the state in which the mind has ceased as a drink or a sleep of bliss that does not lift: Tirumular's drinkers of the nectar of Siva's bliss in the samadhi where the mind melts do not leave it standing, sitting or lying; Pattinathar asks to stay in the drowse of the sleep of bliss, free of thought and of its absence. Tirumular names it samadhi; Pattinathar keeps the word for sleep.

Both make melting the heart of worship: Tirumular commands 'melt your love and praise the Lord' and says Nandi answered when he melted; Pattinathar asks for the heart that breaks and softens into mud, melting and melting, with tears running down the chest. Tirumular reports that it worked; Pattinathar still asks when it will come.

Both refuse to court the rich for a living: Tirumular says do not wither praising petty-minded men for their wealth in hope of sustenance, but praise the Lord with one's true home in mind; Pattinathar refuses to follow the rich, speak of his troubles and show his teeth, and asks instead for solitude at the bound of supreme bliss.

Both make the company of the Lord's people the ground of release: Tirumular says no tapas is needed to make the mind Siva if one has kinship with those whose minds have joined Siva's bliss; Pattinathar says he has stayed where those who praise the Lord are, will not leave the company of the good, and so will not be born again.

311 says forest, air, rags and the begging bowl are nothing without inner love and that true lovers reach release at home. 321 asks for exactly that outward life, house left, begging, toothless, attached to nothing. The two stand together only if 321's begging is the form love takes for this poet, not its substitute; 311 sets the condition under which 321's wish is worth having.

source_issues: Unit 328 (own id siddhar:thiruppadal-thirattu:4.9) carries the shrine label மதுரை and addresses Sokkanatha, but is numbered as the ninth verse of the திருக்கைலாயம் set.
